title: Central isogenies of semisimple groups are multiplicative
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups below are affine $F$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Smoothness and connectedness are as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. A semisimple group means a smooth connected affine group of finite type with no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal closed subgroup scheme; solvable means that successive derived subgroup schemes eventually become trivial, where the derived subgroup is the smallest closed subgroup through which the commutator morphism factors. A multiplicative isogeny is a homomorphism $f:G\to H$ for which $F[H]\to F[G]$ is faithfully flat and whose scheme-theoretic kernel is finite and diagonalizable. Faithfully flat means that extension of scalars is exact and detects zero modules. Finite means finite-dimensional coordinate algebra. Diagonalizable means isomorphic to $D(M)=\operatorname{Spec}F[M]$ for a finite abelian group $M$, where $F[M]$ has basis $e^m$, multiplication $e^me^n=e^{m+n}$, comultiplication $e^m\mapsto e^m\otimes e^m$, counit $e^m\mapsto1$ and antipode $e^m\mapsto e^{-m}$. Let $G_1,G_0$ be semisimple and let $f:G_1\to G_0$ be a homomorphism that is surjective on underlying schemes and has finite central scheme-theoretic kernel. Central means that kernel elements commute with every group element after every commutative $F$-algebra extension. Then $f$ is a multiplicative isogeny. No separability or prime-to-characteristic hypothesis on its kernel is imposed.

source.place: Proposition 19.15 and its proof, printed pp.400--401; Definition 18.1 and following paragraph, printed p.387; faithful flatness of surjective homomorphisms onto smooth groups is Proposition 5.47, printed p.111.

proof.text: Write $A=F[G_0]$ and $B=F[G_1]$. For $y\in G_0(F)$, the affine fibre is $\operatorname{Spec}C$ with $C=B\otimes_{A,y^*}F$ by [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra]. It is nonempty: scheme-surjectivity gives a point $x$ above the underlying point of $y$, and the maps $B\to\kappa(x)$ and $F\to\kappa(x)$ agree on $A$, hence give a map $C\to\kappa(x)$. Thus $C\ne0$. If $b_1,\ldots,b_s$ generate $B$ over $F$, the elements $b_i\otimes1$ generate $C$ over $F$, since every tensor is a sum of $(b\otimes1)(1\otimes c)$. Choose a maximal ideal of $C$ using [lem-weil-common-extension-fields-maximal-ideal]. Clause (1) of [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing] gives an $F$-algebra map $C\to F$. Its composite with $B\to C$ gives an $F$-point above $y$ by [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Therefore $G_1(F)\to G_0(F)$ is surjective.

source.place: Proposition 5.47 and proof, printed p.110; explicit affine-fibre verification of its rational-point hypothesis, using the same Nullstellensatz input.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-affine-group-homomorphism-image] to $f$. Both groups are affine of finite type over the algebraically closed field $F$, the target $G_0$ is smooth by semisimplicity, and step 1 gives surjectivity on $F$-points. Hence the coordinate-algebra map $F[G_0]\to F[G_1]$ is faithfully flat in exactly the sense required by the statement.

The source $G_1$ is reductive. Indeed let $U$ be any smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup of $G_1$. By [lem-sfb-smooth-unipotent-solvable] it has a finite series $U=U_0\supseteq\cdots\supseteq U_d=1$ with commutative quotients. By [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] the quotient homomorphism $U_i\to U_i/U_{i+1}$ has scheme-theoretic kernel $U_{i+1}$; since that quotient is commutative, the commutator morphism of $U_i$ composed with it is trivial, so the commutator factors through the closed subgroup $U_{i+1}$ and the derived subgroup of $U_i$ lies in $U_{i+1}$. Moreover $H\subseteq H'$ implies $D(H)\subseteq D(H')\cap H$. Inductively $D^i(U)\subseteq U_i$, so $D^d(U)=1$. Thus $U$ is solvable also in the derived-series sense used in this item, and semisimplicity forces $U=1$. This is the reductivity condition in [lem-sfb-reductive-centre-multiplicative-type]. Since $F$ is already algebraically closed, its own algebraic closure may be chosen to be $F$, so connectedness and the geometric conditions there require no further extension.

source.place: Proposition 14.21, printed pp.284--285; Proposition 6.30 and its proof, printed p.131; Chapter 19(b), printed p.400.

proof.text: Put $K=\ker f$. By [lem-sc-kernel-subgroup], $K\hookrightarrow G_1$ is a closed subgroup scheme. By [lem-sfb-affine-group-centre-base-change], the universal centre functor is represented by a closed subgroup $Z(G_1)\hookrightarrow G_1$. The centrality hypothesis gives $K(R)\subseteq Z(G_1)(R)$ for every $F$-algebra $R$, including after every further algebra extension. Evaluate this inclusion on the universal point of the affine scheme $K$: it gives the factorization $K\to Z(G_1)\to G_1$ by [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. This factor map is a closed immersion: the surjection $F[G_1]\to F[K]$ factors through the quotient $F[Z(G_1)]$, so $F[Z(G_1)]\to F[K]$ is surjective [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Step 3 and [lem-sfb-reductive-centre-multiplicative-type] give a closed immersion $Z(G_1)\hookrightarrow\mathbf G_m^r$ over $F$ for some $r\geq0$. Composing the two surjective coordinate maps exhibits $K$ as a closed subgroup scheme of this split torus.

source.place: Definition 18.1 and following paragraph, printed p.387; Proposition 1.92, printed pp.33--34; Corollary 17.62(a), printed p.372.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-split-torus-subgroups-diagonalizable] to the closed subgroup $K\subseteq\mathbf G_m^r$ obtained in step 4. It gives $K\simeq\operatorname{Spec}F[M]$ with the displayed group-algebra Hopf structure. Since $F[K]$ is finite-dimensional by hypothesis, its final clause says that $M$ is finite. Together with faithful flatness from step 2, these are precisely the defining conditions for $f$ to be a multiplicative isogeny. The argument imposed neither reducedness on $K$ nor a restriction on its order.
